title: The seed that grows while you sleep (Mark 4:21–34)
hookLine: a lamp on its stand, and seed that grows though the sower doesn't know how

lines: A BEAN IN A PAPER CUP.
cards: A bean in a paper cup at school, tomatoes on a balcony: if you've ever planted anything, you know the temptation. You check it every morning. You want to dig it up a little to see if anything's happening.
You water it too much. Nothing you do makes it go faster. Then one day there's a green thread poking out of the dirt, and you didn't see it happen.
It happened at night, or while you were at work, without you. Jesus told a parable about exactly that, and only Mark kept it.

teach.b: Jesus is still teaching from the boat, with a handful of short sayings and parables. First, the lamp. Nobody lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel basket or under a bed; you put it on the lampstand.
What's hidden is meant to come to light.

teach.h: THE SEED GROWS, HE KNOWS NOT HOW.
teach.b: Second, the seed that grows by itself, only in Mark.
In the Douay-Rheims: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, And should sleep, and rise, night and day, and the seed should spring, and grow up whilst he knoweth not."
"For the earth of itself bringeth forth fruit, first the blade, then the ear, afterwards the full corn in the ear."
Of itself: in Greek, automatē, the word English turned into automatic. Third, what it means. The farmer's work is real: he sows, and when it's ripe, he harvests.
But the growing isn't his. Christians hear this about the kingdom of God, and about faith in a person's life: it grows in stages, often unseen, and it isn't all up to you.
For anyone who worries they're not doing enough, that's a relief. Fourth, the mustard seed.

teach.h: THE SMALLEST SEED, THE BIGGEST SHADE.
teach.b: The kingdom is like the smallest of seeds that becomes a plant so large birds can nest in its shade.

teach.h: FIRST THE BLADE, THEN THE EAR.
teach.b: Small beginnings, hidden growth, a surprising size. Mark says Jesus taught many parables like these, and explained everything privately to his disciples.

how: Catholics hear the parables of the growing seed and the mustard seed at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and often read them as a lesson in patience and trust in God's work.

o: of itself, growing on its own
springing up fast, all at once

games.q: what's inside the parables — tap the pairs.
p: on its stand, not under a bed
the smallest, with the biggest shade

s: the seed growing secretly is in all four gospels
the farmer in the parable still sows and harvests
his work is real; the growing just isn't his.
the English word automatic comes from a Greek word in this parable
automatē, of itself: the earth bears fruit of itself.

games.q: you've sown your field. the harvest is months away. what does the farmer in Jesus's parable do?
o: dig up the seeds to check on them.
sleep and rise, night and day, while it grows he knows not how.
sow the field again, just in case.
games.why: he sleeps and rises, and the seed springs up and grows, he knows not how. the earth bears fruit of itself.

practice: Think of something you've planted and keep digging up to check on: a friendship you're trying to mend, a kid finding their way, a habit you've started, a prayer you keep praying.
Picture it as a seed in dark soil; you've done your part, so let it be. If you pray, hand it to God to grow; if you don't, practice not checking on it, for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Automatē. Greek for of itself, the root of our word automatic, Mark's parable of the kingdom that grows unseen, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: of itself, by itself; the root of the English word automatic.

carryVoice: Your line: it grows while you sleep. Not all of it is up to you. That's day two hundred two.
